prompt: Textbooks say normal human body temperature is $98.6^\circ$F. A random sample of $49$ healthy adults has mean $\bar{x} = 98.2^\circ$F and standard deviation $s = 0.7^\circ$F. For the test of $H_0: \mu = 98.6$ versus $H_a: \mu \ne 98.6$, what is the value of the $t$ statistic?
hint: The $t$ statistic counts how many standard errors the sample mean lies from $98.6$. The sample mean is below that value, so think about the sign.

hints.text: The $t$ statistic counts how many standard errors the sample mean lies from $98.6$. The sample mean is below that value, so think about the sign.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with easier numbers: $\bar{x} = 9$, $\mu_0 = 10$, $s = 2$ and $n = 4$. The standard error is $2/\sqrt{4} = 1$, so $t = (9 - 10)/1 = -1$. Follow the same steps here.
The standard error is $0.7/\sqrt{49} = 0.7/7 = 0.1$. Then compute $t = (98.2 - 98.6)/0.1$, keeping the negative sign.
$t = -0.4/0.1 = -4$, so the sample mean is $4$ standard errors below $98.6$ and the $t$ statistic is $-4$.

explanation: The standard error of the mean is $s/\sqrt{n} = 0.7/7 = 0.1$ degrees.
The sample mean differs from the null value by $\bar{x} - \mu_0 = 98.2 - 98.6 = -0.4$ degrees.
Dividing gives $t = -0.4/0.1 = -4$, with df $= 48$. A sample mean 4 standard errors below 98.6 is very unlikely if $H_0$ is true, so there is convincing evidence the true mean is not $98.6^\circ$F.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the sign matters
steps: $|t| = 4$ sets how surprising the result is; the sign says WHICH way the data lean.
Negative $t$: the sample mean is below the hypothesized $98.6$.
For the two-sided test the $p$-value uses both tails, but you still report $t = -4$ so a reader knows body temperatures came out lower.
